I’ve got 10.1 mu of decent flat land here in Quzhou, and after ten years of growing cotton, I know this soil and this crop well enough to trust my own judgment. My household has four people—myself, my wife, our child, and my father. My wife picks up work at a packaging factory in town whenever the farm isn’t too busy, which gives us some steady cash, but it means I’m the one in the field most days. My father helps watch the child and can still lend a hand at sowing and harvest, but I can’t rely on heavy family labor during the peak season. That’s why I keep things straightforward and stick to what works.

Come spring, as soon as the soil warms in April, I’ll run the rotary tiller across the whole plot to break up the ground and level it. I always lay plastic mulch afterwards—our agricultural extension office has promoted it for years, and I’ve seen for myself that it keeps moisture in and helps the seedlings survive the cool nights. For seed, I’ll buy the certified Bt hybrid from the county supply cooperative. The seed costs more than traditional types, but the bollworm resistance pays for itself because I don’t have to spray expensive chemicals for the main pest.

For fertilizer, I’ll spread compound fertilizer before tillage as a base dressing, then top-dress with urea when the plants start flowering. Over the season I’ll put down about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus roughly 6 kg of phosphorus and 7 kg of potassium—the land here isn’t exhausted yet, but cotton takes nutrients out, so I have to feed it. Water comes from my well, and I’ll irrigate four times: at sowing if the spring is dry, again at the seedling stage, once at early flowering when the plants are thirsty, and a final time at peak boll-setting in July. If the summer turns unusually dry I might add a fifth, but four has usually been enough.

Even with Bt cotton, I still need to watch for aphids, spider mites, and the occasional fungal issue, so I’ll spray pesticides five times through the season. That includes a herbicide before mulching and then targeted insecticide or fungicide sprays as needed. If the weather cooperates and we don’t get heavy autumn rains that stain the open bolls, I expect to bring in about 280 kg of seed cotton per mu. That’s a solid, realistic yield for this area, and it should cover my costs and leave enough profit to get through the year.
